title: Bill Maker
context: Grade 4, the adding half of the chapter's middle section. An adult sees a shop bill added up, which looks like ordinary column addition. What is actually being settled is where each digit goes: the dots in one line, so rupees stand under rupees and paise under paise, and a hundred paise carried as one rupee. The first summary box says two zeros go after the dot whenever there are no paise, and the later box puts them in the paise column; the pages themselves write whole amounts with no dot. This tool uses the later form, so two zeros appear only in column working, where they keep a whole-rupee price's rupees in the rupees column.

writeup.why: Put prices on a bill with every dot in one line, carry each hundred paise as one rupee, and total the bill at its foot.
writeup.look: A bill slip down the middle of the canvas with its dotted line between rupees and paise, a shop shelf of price cards beside it, and a carry circle over the rupees column.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Bill Maker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the lines priced against the lines this bill needs, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each price card snaps onto its line and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The shop shelf stands at the left of the working area, 300 by 500 at 64,214, holding price cards, each 260 by 56, with the thing's name in ink and its price written with a dot. The bill slip stands in the middle, 440 by 500 at 384,214, on the panel colour: the word Bill at its head, then a line for each thing bought, the thing's name at the left and a price column at the right, 220 wide, split by the near-black dotted line into rupees on its left and paise on its right, with the headings Rs and p above it outside the working. Carry circles sit in a row over the rupees column, one over each place, empty until something is carried. A near-black rule crosses the column under the last line, and the Total line sits under the rule. A price card dragged onto a line snaps so that its dot lands on the dotted line, rupees under rupees and paise under paise; a card set down with its dot off the line springs back to the shelf with the dotted line lit, and a pale outline of where it was set stays standing on the slip. A whole-rupee price snaps in with two zeros in its paise column, grey and at full weight. The paise box stands at the right, 280 by 120 at 870,214, and shows the paise column's sum as a number of paise before anything is carried. When that sum is a hundred or more, each hundred gathers into a full strip of a hundred cells, rolls up into one rupee and drops into the carry circle over the rupees, and only what is left, as two digits, goes down into the paise column. The add control sits under the paise box, 280 by 60 at 870,350, and works the paise column first and the rupees with the carry second, and the answer line carries the dotted line on down, so the dot of the total lands under the dots above it. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a dot key, and the answer slot prints Rs before the number and holds exactly two places after the dot, so a paise sum of three digits has nowhere to be written but the carry circle. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue. The paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion, a clear round dot, and wherever amounts stand in columns it sits on a near-black dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count of things is not money. The zeros that fill the paise column of a whole-rupee amount in column working are grey. Every play note is one plain pale blue rectangle and every play coin one plain steel disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, each printed with its value and nothing else. No coin below one rupee is drawn anywhere: paise are shaded cells on a strip ruled into a hundred in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every column rule, dotted line, tick, bracket, strike line, bill rule and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in, a count by the box beside the times sign or the slot marked things, and the change or money left by the tray or line that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in a paise column is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. Every price on the slip sits with its dot on the one dotted line, so rupees can only stand under rupees. The carry circle takes one rupee for each full hundred paise and nothing smaller, and a carried rupee stays in its circle after the rupees are added, so the working can be read afterwards.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last bill the child made, every price on its line with the dots in a column, each carry in its circle, and the total at the foot.

phases.win: the dots stand in one straight line, and each column adds on its own
phases.does: drags each price onto a line so its dot lands on the dotted line, then adds the paise column and the rupees column
phases.goal: amounts are added in columns with the dots in one straight line, so rupees sit under rupees and paise under paise
phases.says: Put each price on the bill. Where must the dots sit?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write Rs 125.40 under Rs 32.15 with the dots in one line, and add them.
phases.feels: once every dot sits on one line, each column holds only one kind of money
phases.hands: Write Rs 214.35 and Rs 43.20 on the board one under the other, first lined up at their left edges and then with their dots in one column. Ask the class to add each version and to say which digits were added to which. Then circle the dots in the second version and draw a line down through them.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: where is each price's dot? Second rung, the phase's: which digits stand under the rupees of the first price? Third rung: the slip is cut to two prices with the same number of rupee digits, and the child adds them before the longer price comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: writing starts at the left of a line, and the two prices look like two rows of digits to be stacked.
wrong.move: starts both prices at the left edge, so the five of fifty-two stands under the three of three hundred and fourteen and the dots do not line up.
wrong.screen: the Rs 52.60 card springs back from where the child set it, and the dotted line lights, with a pale outline left standing where the card was, its dot one place left of the line. The card then snaps in with its dot on the line, fifty-two under the fourteen of three hundred and fourteen, and the outline stays standing beside it.

wrong.why: the digits come out of the adding one column at a time, and the dot is not a digit, so nothing in the adding writes it.
wrong.move: adds every column correctly and writes the total with no dot, 36685, which reads as thirty-six thousand six hundred and eighty-five rupees.
wrong.screen: the dotted line runs on down through the answer line and lights there, and the child's digits are laid across it: the eight and the five fall to the right of the line in green, and three hundred and sixty-six stands to its left in deep blue. The vermilion dot drops onto the line between them, and the child's number stays in the slot.

phases.screen: an empty bill slip with its dotted line, and two price cards on the shelf
phases.soWhat: Line up the dots, and rupees fall under rupees and paise under paise.
phases.concept: Rupees under rupees, paise under paise

phases.win: a hundred paise roll up into the carry circle as one rupee, and the paise column shows only what is left
phases.does: adds the paise, sees the sum pass a hundred, carries one rupee, writes the rest, and adds the rupees with the carry
phases.goal: when the paise add to a hundred or more, each hundred is carried as one rupee and only the paise left are written
phases.says: The paise come to more than a hundred. What happens to the hundred?
phases.check: Add Rs 24.80 and Rs 13.40. What is written in the paise column, and what is carried?
phases.feels: a hundred paise are too many for the paise column, so they go and join the rupees
phases.hands: Shade eighty cells on one paper strip and forty on another. Ask a child to shade the same hundred and twenty cells onto fresh strips, filling one before starting the next: one strip fills and twenty cells are left. Swap the full strip for a rupee coin, then write the sum in columns, twenty in the paise column and one rupee carried.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do the paise add up to? Second rung, the phase's: is that more than a hundred? Third rung: the slip is cut to two prices whose paise make just over a hundred, and the child carries before the larger sum comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the paise sum is one number, and splitting a number that has just been made feels wrong.
wrong.move: writes all of one hundred and forty in the paise column and gets Rs 175.140.
wrong.screen: the paise box shows one hundred and forty paise, and a hundred of its cells gather into a full strip that rolls up into one rupee and drops into the carry circle, leaving forty below. The child's three places after the dot are laid on the answer line, and the third has no place to stand. The rupees are added again with the carry, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: once the forty is written the paise column looks finished, and the small one in the carry circle is easy to leave behind.
wrong.move: carries the rupee from one hundred and forty paise but forgets to add it, and writes Rs 175.40.
wrong.screen: the carry circle over the rupees column glows amber with its one still in it, and the rupees column is added again with the circle's rupee travelling down into the sum: one hundred and twenty-eight and forty-seven make one hundred and seventy-five, and one more makes one hundred and seventy-six. The child's answer stays in the slot beside it.

phases.screen: two prices on the slip whose paise add to more than a hundred, with the carry circle empty
phases.soWhat: Each hundred paise is carried as one rupee, and only the paise left are written, as two digits.
phases.concept: A hundred paise carry one rupee

phases.win: two zeros fill the paise column, the rupees stay in line, and the sum comes out right
phases.does: places the whole-rupee price, fills its paise column with two zeros, and adds
phases.goal: in column working, an amount with no paise gets two zeros in its paise column, so its rupees stay in the rupees column
phases.says: This price has no paise. What goes in its paise column?
phases.check: Add Rs 48 and Rs 21.35 in columns. What goes in the paise column for the forty-eight?
phases.feels: the grey zeros hold the paise column open, so the rupees cannot slip across the dot
phases.hands: Write Rs 35 and Rs 12.50 on the board and ask the class to add them in columns. If anyone sets the thirty-five under the fifty paise, fill its paise column with two zeros, 35.00, and add again. Then write the answer in a sentence, Rs 47.50, and point out that a whole amount in a sentence, such as Rs 35, is written with no dot: the zeros belong to the column working.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which price has no paise? Second rung, the phase's: what goes in its paise column? Third rung: the slip is cut to one short whole-rupee price under one short price with paise, and the child fills the empty paise places before adding. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a number with no dot is lined up at the right like any whole number, and there it lands under the paise.
wrong.move: writes the twenty-nine of Rs 29 under the paise and adds twenty-nine paise, so rupees are added to paise and the sum comes out as Rs 63.74.
wrong.screen: the Rs 29 card springs back from under the paise, its outline left standing there, and snaps in again with grey zeros filling its paise column and its twenty-nine under the sixty-three. The paise column adds forty-five and nothing, the rupees add to ninety-two, and the child's Rs 63.74 stays in the slot beside the new line.

wrong.why: with nothing written under the forty-five, the paise column looks as if it needs no adding.
wrong.move: adds the rupees and stops at Rs 92, leaving off the forty-five paise because the whole-rupee price seemed to have no paise to add.
wrong.screen: the two zeros in the whole-rupee price's paise column light grey, and the paise column is added with them, forty-five and nothing making forty-five, which goes down into the answer line in green. The answer line then reads rupees, dot and paise all filled, and the child's Rs 92 stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a price with paise already on the slip, and a whole-rupee price card waiting on the shelf
phases.soWhat: In column working, an amount with no paise gets two zeros in its paise column. In a sentence it is written with no dot, as Rs 29.
phases.concept: Two zeros when there are no paise

phases.win: the total lands at the foot of the bill under the rule
phases.does: writes each thing and its price on a line of the bill, adds the columns with every carry, and writes the total at the foot
phases.goal: a bill lists each thing bought with its price, and the total is added at the foot
phases.says: Write each thing and its price. What goes at the foot of the bill?
phases.check: Make a bill for a ruler at Rs 18.50, glue at Rs 26.75 and a notebook at Rs 45. What goes at the foot?
phases.feels: a bill is a column of prices with one sum at its foot, however many lines it has
phases.hands: Set up a class shop with priced packets. One child buys three things and writes the bill: the word Bill at the top, one thing and its price to a line, the dots in one column, a rule, and the total at the foot. A second child checks it by adding the prices in a different order.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: has every price been written on the bill? Second rung, the phase's: what did the paise column carry? Third rung: the bill is cut to two lines, and the child totals them before the other lines come back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a bill of three lines has a lot to add, and the carry is made in one column and needed in the other.
wrong.move: forgets the rupee carried from the paise and writes Rs 270.65 at the foot of the bill.
wrong.screen: the paise box shows one hundred and sixty-five paise, a full strip rolls up into the carry circle, and sixty-five goes down. The rupees column is then added with the circle's rupee travelling down into it, and the Total line reads the new sum beside the child's Rs 270.65, which stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the carries met before this one were each a single rupee, so one feels like what a carry is.
wrong.move: carries one rupee when the paise of four prices come to two hundred and eighty, and writes Rs 298.80.
wrong.screen: the paise box shows two hundred and eighty paise, and two full strips fill one after the other, each rolling up into a rupee, so the carry circle reads two. Eighty goes down into the paise column, the rupees are added with both carried rupees, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside the new total.

phases.screen: a shop shelf of three or four priced things and an empty bill slip
phases.soWhat: A bill lists each thing bought and its price, one to a line, and the total goes at the foot.

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the paise box passes a hundred. The cells of the paise sum pour into a strip, filling it block by block until it holds exactly a hundred, and the full strip curls up into one rupee that rises and drops into the carry circle, while the paise left slide down into the paise column as two green digits. When the sum passes two hundred, two strips fill and curl up one after the other, and the carry circle reads two. The add can be undone and run again as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the bill slip is empty, its dotted line drawn down the price column, and two price cards stand on the shelf. On the second two prices already stand on the slip with their dots in line, the paise box empty and the carry circle open. On the third one price with paise stands on the slip and a whole-rupee price card waits on the shelf. On the fourth the shelf holds three or four priced things and the bill slip is empty down to its rule. The running count at the top left holds the lines priced against the lines this bill needs, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: a price card, or the paise box, or the whole-rupee card, or the first line of the slip, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where each dot belongs. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any prices on any number of lines, with the carry circle and the total open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on lining up the dots, carrying a hundred paise, whole-rupee prices in column working, and making bills.
voiceLines: An empty bill and a shelf of prices. Where does each dot belong?
Put each price on the bill. Where must the dots sit?
The paise come to more than a hundred. What happens to the hundred?
This price has no paise. What goes in its paise column?
Write each thing and its price. What goes at the foot of the bill?
A new bill. Look at every dot before you add.
Free play. Any prices on any lines, with the carry circle and the total open.
Lay the prices again with the dots in line, and add the paise first.
Every dot in one line, every hundred paise carried, and every bill totalled at its foot.

observations.why: With the dots in one line, the rupees of every price stand in one column and the paise in another.
observations.soWhat: Line up the dots, and rupees fall under rupees and paise under paise.
observations.observe: Every card snapped with its dot on the dotted line, and each column added on its own.

observations.why: A hundred paise are one rupee, so they belong with the rupees and cannot stay in a column of two digits.
observations.soWhat: Each hundred paise is carried as one rupee, and only the paise left are written, as two digits.
observations.observe: Each time the paise passed a hundred, a full strip rolled into the carry circle as one rupee.

observations.why: The zeros fill the paise places, so the price's rupees cannot slide into the paise column.
observations.soWhat: In column working, an amount with no paise gets two zeros in its paise column.
observations.observe: The whole-rupee card came in with grey zeros under the paise, and its rupees stayed under the rupees.

observations.why: A bill is a list of prices added in one column, so its total is a sum like any other.
observations.soWhat: A bill lists each thing bought and its price, one to a line, and the total goes at the foot.
observations.observe: The total landed under the rule, with each carry still in its circle above it.

serves.exercise: making three bills and finding the total money due on each

source_tool.description: A bill pad fills the stage: a slip with a line for each thing bought and a price column split by a dotted line into rupees on the left and paise on the right, with a rule and a Total line at its foot. Price cards are dragged from a shop shelf onto the lines of the slip, and each card snaps so its dot lands on the dotted line, rupees under rupees and paise under paise. A price with no paise snaps in with its paise column filled by two zeros, drawn in the same ink as every other digit. The add control works the paise column first and writes the paise sum in a box beside the slip. When the sum reaches a hundred or more, each hundred rolls up as one rupee into a carry circle over the rupees column, and only what is left, as two digits, is written in the paise column. The rupees column is then added with the carry, and the total is written at the foot of the bill.
source_tool.art_direction: A shop bill, dots in one line / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.note: THERE IS NO MODE AXIS ON THIS TOOL FAMILY. learn, practice and freeplay are gone and are not replaced by three of anything else: the axis itself is wrong for a tool a child works alone. See phase_mount.

authored.freeplay: Free Play. Any prices on any number of lines, with the carry circle and the total open.
authored.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items on lining up the dots, carrying a hundred paise, whole-rupee prices in column working, and making bills.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a rupee tray and a paise tray, strips ruled into a hundred cells, a counting tray of value slots, a bill slip with a dotted line, a shop counter with a change tray, a multiplying frame under a row of things, and a till with a share mat.

Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else: no design, no picture, no lettering but the value. Every note is a plain paper rectangle and every coin a plain metal disc, all notes one size and one colour and all coins one size and one metal, so a value is read from its print and never from size or colour.

No coin below one rupee is drawn or named anywhere. Wherever paise are drawn rather than written, they are shaded cells on a rupee strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Nothing standing for paise is ever round.

Written money with paise is Rs, the rupees, a dot and two digits of paise, as Rs 96.75. Fewer than ten paise are written with a zero in the first place after the dot. A whole amount in running text is written with no dot, as Rs 43.

Column working always stands on a dotted line: every dot in a column sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right. In column working a whole-rupee amount carries two zeros in its paise column, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit.

A hundred paise rolling up into one rupee is always shown moving, from the paise column into a small carry circle over the rupees, and a rupee broken into paise is always shown opening into a full strip of a hundred cells.
A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through and the new figure written above it, never erased, so the break can be read afterwards.
The number of things in a product is a count. It stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, with no dot, and no cell exists for it under the paise.
Every answer slot carries its unit, rupees or things, printed beside the number.
A total, a change, a cost or an amount left is told apart by the slot or line it sits in first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a note, a coin, a cell or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue, and the paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion in every tool, drawn as a clear round dot on the dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count is never money. The two zeros in the paise column of a whole-rupee amount are grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded. Every play note is one plain pale blue and every play coin one plain steel, so a value is read from its print and never from its colour. All of that holds in greyscale, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in and a count by the box beside the times sign, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lay the prices again with the dots in line, and add the paise first.
voice.onNext: A new bill. Look at every dot before you add.
voice.opening: An empty bill and a shelf of prices. Where does each dot belong?
voice.onFinish: Every dot in one line, every hundred paise carried, and every bill totalled at its foot.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any prices on any lines, with the carry circle and the total open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Rupees under rupees, paise under paise
A hundred paise carry one rupee
Two zeros when there are no paise

placement.where: After a class shop has been set up with priced packets and one bill has been written out by hand, one thing to a line. The tool is what snaps every dot onto one line and rolls a hundred paise up into the rupees, which a bill on paper leaves to the child's care.

answer_key.rule: To add money, write the amounts one under another with the dots in one straight line, so rupees stand under rupees and paise under paise. Add the paise column first. When the paise come to a hundred or more, each hundred is carried as one rupee to the rupees column, and only the paise left are written, as two digits. Then add the rupees with anything carried. In column working, an amount with no paise is written with two zeros in its paise column, so its rupees stay in the rupees column; in running text a whole amount is written with no dot. A bill lists each thing bought with its price, one to a line, and the total is added at its foot.
answer_key.wrong: The price cards are lifted off and set down again one line at a time with their dots on the dotted line, and the paise column is added again with each hundred rolling up in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write Rs 52.60 under Rs 314.25 with the dots in one line, so 52 stands under the 14 of 314.
Paise first: 25 and 60 make 85 paise, less than a hundred, so nothing is carried.
Rupees: 314 and 52 make 366. The sum is Rs 366.85.
items.question: Add Rs 314.25 and Rs 52.60.
items.checkpoint: Line up the dots, and rupees fall under rupees and paise under paise.
items.misconception: Starting both amounts at the left edge, so the 5 of 52 stands under the 3 of 314 and the dots do not line up.

steps: 140 paise is 1 rupee and 40 paise, so write 40 in the paise column and carry 1 rupee.
Rupees: 128 and 47 make 175, and the 1 carried makes 176. The sum is Rs 176.40.
items.question: Add Rs 128.65 and Rs 47.75.
items.checkpoint: When the paise come to a hundred or more, carry one rupee for each hundred and write only the paise left.
items.misconception: Writing all of 140 in the paise column, which gives Rs 175.140, a price with three places after the dot.

steps: Rs 29 has no paise, so in column working it is written 29.00, with two zeros in the paise column.
Rupees: 63 and 29 make 92. The sum is Rs 92.45.
items.question: Add Rs 63.45 and Rs 29 in columns.
items.checkpoint: In column working, an amount with no paise gets two zeros in its paise column, and its rupees stay in the rupees column.
items.misconception: Writing the 29 under the paise and adding 29 paise, which gives Rs 63.74.

steps: Write each thing and its price on its own line, with the dots in one column.
Paise first: 50, 75 and 40 make 165 paise, so write 65 and carry 1 rupee.
Rupees: 145, 89 and 36 make 270, and the 1 carried makes 271. The total at the foot of the bill is Rs 271.65.
items.question: Make a bill: a lunch box for Rs 145.50, a water bottle for Rs 89.75 and a pencil pouch for Rs 36.40. What is the total?
items.checkpoint: A bill lists each thing bought and its price, with the total added at the foot.
items.misconception: Forgetting the carried rupee and writing Rs 270.65 at the foot of the bill.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.

items.question: Add Rs 506.15 and Rs 71.20.
items.final_answer: Rs 577.35. The 71 stands under the 06 of 506, with the dots in one line

items.question: Add Rs 38.85 and Rs 16.45.
items.final_answer: Rs 55.30. The paise make 130, so 30 is written and 1 rupee is carried

items.question: Add Rs 249.95 and Rs 150.05.
items.final_answer: Rs 400.00, which is Rs 400. The paise make exactly 100, so 00 goes in the paise column and 1 rupee is carried

items.question: Add Rs 74 and Rs 18.35 in columns.
items.final_answer: Rs 92.35. In column working, Rs 74 is written 74.00, with two zeros in the paise column

items.question: A child adds Rs 56.20 and Rs 13 and gets Rs 56.33. What went wrong, and what is the sum?
items.final_answer: The 13 was written under the paise. In column working Rs 13 is 13.00, with two zeros in the paise column, and the sum is Rs 69.20

items.question: Make a bill: a kite for Rs 65.50, a reel of thread for Rs 42.75 and a cap for Rs 110. What is the total?
items.final_answer: Rs 218.25. The paise make 125, so 25 is written and 1 rupee is carried; the cap is written 110.00 in the column

items.question: Make a bill: notebooks for Rs 84.60, a geometry box for Rs 132.85, a pen for Rs 24.90 and crayons for Rs 57.45. What is the total?
items.final_answer: Rs 299.80. The paise make 280, so 80 is written and 2 rupees are carried

teaching_notes: Set up a class shop with priced packets and write one bill by hand before the tool is opened, one thing to a line and the dots under each other. Then use the tool for the two moves that slip on paper: every dot on one line, and each hundred paise rolled up into the rupees as one rupee. Say what a bill is, because the chapter highlights the word and never says: a bill lists the things bought and their prices, with the total at the foot. The chapter gives the rule for amounts with no paise twice. The first box says two zeros are written after the dot, and the later box puts them in the paise column. The pages themselves write forty-three rupees and three thousand rupees in running text with no dot, so teach the later form: two zeros belong in column working, where they keep a whole-rupee price's rupees in the rupees column. One printed bill has its words run together with no spaces, so read it aloud before anyone copies it.
generation_prompt: Build a bill-making tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A bill slip stands in the working area with a line for each thing bought and a price column split by a dotted line into rupees on the left and paise on the right, with a rule and a Total line at its foot. A shop shelf beside it holds price cards. A card dragged onto a line snaps so its dot sits on the dotted line, rupees under rupees and paise under paise, and a whole-rupee price snaps in with its paise column filled by two zeros, drawn at full weight like every other digit. An add control works the paise column first and shows its sum in a box beside the slip; when the sum reaches a hundred or more, each hundred rolls up as one rupee into a carry circle over the rupees column, and only the paise left, as two digits, are written below. The rupees column is then added with the carry and the total written on the Total line. A price set down with its dot off the line springs back to the shelf with the dotted line lit, with nothing marked. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put each price on its own line with the dots in one line. Add the paise first. Carry each hundred paise as one rupee. Write the total at the foot.
